passages.text: The Difference Between Introverts and Extroverts Brain scans reveal a physiological difference between quiet thinkers and social butterflies. By Michelle Gallagher published July 1, 1999 - last reviewed on June 4, 2025 Party animals and wallflowers hoping to change their social personas may have no say in the matter. A study shows that introverts and extroverts show activity in different brain structures which mirror the wildly opposing aspects of their personalities. Debra Johnson, Ph.D., and John S. Wiebe, Ph.D., used positron emission tomography (PET) to measure cerebral blood flow—an indicator of brain activity—in individuals rated on a personality test as shy or gregarious. Johnson, a research scientist at the University of Iowa, and Wiebe, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Texas, asked both types to think freely while undergoing PET scans. The images they obtained clearly separated the quiet thinkers from the social butterflies. Introverts showed increased blood flow in the frontal lobes, the anterior thalamus and other structures associated with recalling events, making plans and problem-solving. Extroverts, on the other hand, displayed more activity in the posterior thalamus and posterior insula, regions involved in interpreting sensory data. passages.text: Introverts and extroverts are two contrasting personality types. Carl Gustav Jung introduced both terms in 1910. They sit at opposite ends of a single continuum, and most people fall somewhere between them. Introverts prefer solitude and find energy in alone time, while extroverts thrive on social interaction and seek external stimulation. Key Takeaways - Introversion: Reserve, passivity and thoughtfulness, with a preference for keeping emotional states private. - Introvert Energy: Introverts recharge in solitary or low-stimulus settings. They often prefer one-to-one contact and find heavy socializing draining. - Extroversion: Sociability, assertiveness and cheerfulness. Extroverts seek novelty and excitement and enjoy being the center of attention. - Extrovert Energy: Extroverts are energized by other people. They seek out group activities and may feel restless or isolated when alone too long. - A Spectrum: Neither type is all-or-nothing. Extroversion is a scale, and most people sit somewhere between the two ends. - Changing Type: Your position on the spectrum stays fixed. You can still practice more extroverted behaviors, such as public speaking. What does it mean to be an Introvert? passages.text: Theories of Introversion and Extroversion Introversion is generally viewed as existing as part of a continuum along with extroversion, and most people tend to lie somewhere between the two. For example, they might be outgoing in some situations with some introverted tendencies. Carl Jung Carl Jung was one of the first people to define the terms introvert and extrovert in a psychological context. According to Jung (1910; 1923), personality is based on four pairs of opposing types. He claimed that these types are present in all of us, but one is more dominant than the other, meaning that personality is on four dimensions, which are: - Extroversion/ Introversion - Sensing/ Intuition - Thinking/ Feeling - Judging/ Perceiving Jung[36] described extroverts as preferring to engage with the outside world of objects, sensory perception, and action. Introverts he described differently. They focus on the internal world of reflection, and are thoughtful and insightful. Jung[36] believed a balance between the two best served the goal of self-realization. Modern perspectives on introversion and extroversion focus on behavior, such as sociability and assertiveness. Introverts typically prefer reflection and independence. They thrive in quieter environments and find solitude restorative. Introverts tend to be deep thinkers and good listeners. “Time alone gives introverts an opportunity to get their thoughts together and charge their batteries,” Dr. Tworek notes. And while introversion is sometimes confused with being shy, there’s a difference. Shyness is a fear of being judged negatively by others. Introversion isn’t a matter of confidence or worrying about others’ opinions. It’s simply about preferring to have time for yourself to look inward and process your thoughts. In other words, not all introverts are shy, and not all people who are shy are introverts. Not every introvert checks all the boxes. But if several of these traits sound familiar, you may lean more toward the introverted side of the spectrum: - You enjoy spending time alone or in small groups of people you know well. - You’re a thoughtful listener. - You prefer deep, one-on-one conversations over large group dynamics. - You avoid conflict. - You think before speaking. He framed the types as perspectives: introverts view the world subjectively, extroverts view it objectively. That framing is arguably a weakness. It describes how introverts and extroverts see, not what they do. Jung’s[36] view of extroverted and introverted types serves as a basis for the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI). This questionnaire describes a person’s degree of introversion versus extroversion, thinking versus feeling, intuition versus sensation, and judging versus perceiving[37]. Hans Eysenck Hans Eysenck (1947; 1966; 1967) constructed a theory of personality which has a biological basis. He believed that personality was the result of biological differences in individuals’ nervous systems which ultimately affect their ability to learn and adapt to the environment. Eysenck proposed that personality could be represented by three dimensions: - Introversion/Extroversion (E) - Neuroticism/Stability (N) - Psychoticism/Normality (P) Eysenck argued that each personality trait traces back to a different biological cause. In particular, he held that personality depends on a balance between excitation and inhibition of the autonomic nervous system. That mechanism needs unpacking. Cultural Differences The introversion-extroversion dimension is one that has been shown to be measured reliably across the globe, although there are distinct differences between cultural groups. Western cultures show a clear bias towards extroverts. In the United States and the United Kingdom, people are taught from a young age that being sociable makes you happy[2]. That bias reaches the workplace. Employees who are not extroverted can end up feeling negatively about their job when their employer favors the more outgoing and assertive[27]. Their participants empathized with positive and negative facial expressions while an electroencephalogram (EEG) measured their responses. They found a higher frequency of cortical arousal in introverts than in extroverts. This supports Eysenck’s theory of different cortical arousal levels. It may also explain why extroverts need more external stimulation, because they can become easily bored. Later fMRI work agrees. Lei, Yang and Wu (2015) used fMRI while participants completed cognitive tasks. Extroversion was associated with activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the middle temporal gyrus and the amygdala. These areas handle memory, attention and emotional response. Extrovert Strengths and Trade-Offs Extroverts’ strong suits lie in their ability to be outgoing and interactive with the outside world. This social and bubbly personality helps them in cases like job opportunities[7] and meeting new individuals. However, extroverts also crave new adventures and are impulsive. They seek novelty and excitement, and can feel restless or isolated when alone for too long. Their impulsivity can lead to behavior that some studies show to be linked with “lower rational decision-making styles”[8]. Its sample was 296 Lebanese medical students. Both personality types have advantageous qualities that make them valuable to society, as well as attributes that can be negative. Extroverts and introverts are both good in their own ways. No “better” or “worse” personality type exists. Variance in personalities is itself useful, because both play crucial roles in balancing the flow of social interactions. What is an Ambivert? Is It Better To Be An Extrovert Or An Introvert? Both extroverts and introverts have unique characteristics that might make them look more appealing than the other. For example, maybe a large friend group that comes with being extroverted is important to you. Or perhaps the lifestyle of deep thought that introverts practice is more your style. Still, each personality has strengths and weaknesses crucial to its place on the personality spectrum. passages.text: Leaders and Employee Proactivity Extroverts take more leadership roles, but that does not always make them the better leader. It depends on the team. Grant, Gino and Hofmann (2011) ran a field study with a national pizza-delivery chain and a follow-up laboratory experiment. The best leader depended on the team: - Passive employees: Extroverted leadership predicted higher profits only when employees were relatively passive. - Proactive employees: Teams led by introverts were more profitable. - Why introverts won: Those leaders listened. They were more likely to act on employee suggestions rather than override them with their own enthusiasm. A daily-diary study of 197 leaders across ten working days adds the mechanism[19]. More introverted leaders expected discomfort at acting extroverted. That expectation, not any lack of ability, reduced how much extroverted behavior they enacted. Their leader-like behavior held up. Setting direction and taking charge were unaffected. Introverted leaders do not need to perform extroversion to be effective. Introversion and Autism Are Not the Same Autism and introversion are often confused. Both can involve a wish for time alone. The reasons differ. An introvert typically seeks solitude to recharge from ordinary social stimulation. An autistic person’s withdrawal is more often recovery from sensory overload or from the effort of decoding social cues.
